topComments.author: jmyeet
topComments.text: I'm generally supportive of the idea of banning advertising to children. This would remove the financial incentive for a lot of bad behavior (IMHO). It's also a much cleaner solution and (IMHO) more likely to survive any First Amendment challenges. Speaking of which, these laws will end up going to the Supreme Court on First Amendment grounds and I, for one, am interested to see how that's resolved because the industry as a whole doesn't like either outcome. Let me explain. The central argument will be that an algorithm is expression so any government limits on that violates the First Amendment. Currently that argument is not settled law. None of this is. If the courts rule it is not expression then the laws will stand and social media companies will not be happy. But let's say that courts take the view that it is expression. Well that too is a problem for Section 230. Let me explain. There was a time when publishers (newspapers in particular, given the year) had strict liability for defamation. That meant that if they published a false statement and it was defamatory they were liable, even if made in error. In a landmark case (NYT v. Sullivan) in 1960 the Supreme Court relaxed that to what's generally called a fault-based standard . It meant that when it came to public figures that alleged victim of defamation had to prove actual malice or reckless disregard for the truth. By extension, strict liability applied to non-public figures. Section 230, without using this specific language, basically distinguishes between platforms and publishers . Publishers means news organizations like NYT, CNN, etc. Another way of describing this is first-party publishers. Platforms means anything hosting third-party content (eg Twitter, Facebook, HN). You can refer to these as third-party publishers. The landmark nature of Section 230 was to remove strict liability for the second kind. This means that if, as a user of HN, post a defamatory statement about a private person then YCombinator is not liable for that (within limits). Here's the problem: I believe that social media companies are "cheating" here. They enjoy the Section 230 third-party protections while acting like first-party publishers. What do I mean by that? An "algorithm" allows them to suppress speech they don't like. Example: let's say users generate a bunch of posts that are either pro-Ukraine or pro-Russia with respect to Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. A news organization can take a position one way or the other but they have liability concerns. Twitter has no liability concerns but they can still take a position by suppressing posts on one side or the other. Back to the original issue, if an algorithm is expression, it weakens this shield that (IMHO) is being abused. I believe that if you're suppressing content as a platform based on the content of that speech, you shouldn't enjoy the same protections as somebody who isn't. If you value free speech, you shouldn't allow social media companies carte blanche to suppress speech, particularly when they do so in lockstep with government policy. Social media companies like doing this and they like not having liability so algorithms being expression undermines all that. They really want these laws to go away without deciding that issue.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Is it undefined behavior if const member function changes *this through its argument?

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Is a hard timeout for asynchronous operations that don’t work with SemaphoreSlim without creating leakages possible?

Releasing in work.ContinueWith(...) : won't violate the concurrency limit, but once 5 calls are hung forever, all the permits will be blocked and the pipeline will be deadlocked indefinitely. Is there some idiomatic approach in .NET for dealing with non-cooperative hung tasks without violating the concurrency limit and starving the semaphore or is process isolation the only solution?

stackOverflowQuestions.title: How to get release versions and dates from PyPI without downloading each release?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I'm using the PyPI JSON API to get releases information for a package; this is available at the 'detail' endpoint . The problem is that I need each existing release number and publishing date; this is actually provided in the field 'releases' of the JSON object. However, this field is marked as deprecated, so I cannot rely on it, despite it having all the information I need. The solution proposed by the PyPI team for this case is to use PyPI index API . So theoretically in this response we can have all the existing releases, each one with its publishing date. But the items don't include the version as a distinct value; it is only available from the distribution filename like in "foo_bar-42.0.tar.gz" and here is another problem because distribution filename has an old legacy and we can encounter filenames like "foo-bar-1.0.tar.gz", "foo_bar-1.0-alpha-1.tar.gz", etc.. I did not find any library that is able to correctly parse a distribution filename (with support for all the legacy) and I did not find any information from PyPI that would help to do it or to find another solution. The goal here is to find these information with the fewest request possible; actually i'm making two requests (JSON detail + Index releases) but it is not conceivable to fetch the JSON detail for each available release. I need to do it programmatically with Python because this is for a tool I'm working on. The purpose of this tool is to compute the project requirements lateness: given a list of requirements, for each one it resolves the version that would be installed and find the lateness of this version compared to the latest one available on PyPI.

infoqArticles.description: PyTorch now lets an AI reviewer approve pull requests from its own maintainers. OpenAI, Anthropic and Sonar describe similar ways to automate approval while keeping humans on risky changes. By Andrew Hoblitzell

infoqArticles.description: Netflix developed Quasar, an internal tool that combines semantic code indexing and API comparisons to identify downstream consumers affected by library changes. infoqArticles.title: Presentation: From Fan-Out to Fast: Sub-100ms API Design in Distributed Systems
infoqArticles.description: Saranya Vedagiri explains how to design resilient, low-latency distributed APIs under 100ms. Drawing on practical scale at eBay, she discusses hop-by-hop latency budgets, async fanout tradeoffs, thread pool sizing, caching, and circuit breakers. Learn actionable strategies to eliminate tail-latency bottlenecks and establish performance-first engineering practices. By Saranya Vedagiri
infoqArticles.author: Saranya Vedagiri

infoqArticles.title: Article: Engineering Reliable Telematics from Smartphone Sensors
infoqArticles.description: Smartphones make telematics more accessible by combining location, motion sensors, computing power, and connectivity in a single device. But the convenience comes with a trade-off: device placement varies, sampling behavior is managed by the mobile platform, and measurements have different timing and coordinate semantics. This article explores a six-stage architecture to address these challenges.
infoqArticles.author: Praveen Kumar Gopalakrishnan

infoqArticles.title: Mozilla Partners with Mistral to Bring Open-Weight AI Models to Firefox Smart Window
infoqArticles.description: Mozilla has partnered with Mistral AI to offer Mistral Small 4, an open-weight model, in Firefox's Smart Window AI assistant, now in beta. It is recommended for users in France, the US and Canada. Users can choose among several models, and Mistral agreed to zero data retention. Beta feedback is mixed. By Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review
infoqArticles.description: Ankit Jain of Aviator told QCon San Francisco 2026 that line-by-line code review is already fading, since most review comments concern knowledge sharing rather than defects and over 75% of PRs merge without human review. He proposed six layers: argue, capture, codify, prove, debate, own. His team merges four times more PRs, with about 40% fewer reverts. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: Building a Production-Ready Culture and Skills through SRE-Based Training
infoqArticles.description: Training can act as a confidence engine, turning repeated behaviors into habits and culture. We can tailor training programs that equip developers and operators with the skills to run their services in line with the organization’s maturity and growth, and apply SRE principles to the training itself. She discusses data prep with hard negatives, distributed InfoNCE loss training on H100 GPUs, automated hyperparameter tuning, and production evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge. By Rachel Shalom
infoqArticles.author: Rachel Shalom

infoqArticles.title: .NET MAUI 11 Makes CoreCLR the Default Runtime and Adds Incremental XAML Hot Reload
infoqArticles.description: Microsoft released .NET 11 with a .NET MAUI update focused on product quality. CoreCLR is now the default runtime on all platforms, and XAML gets incremental hot reload, implicit namespaces and faster resource dictionaries. The release also adds device test templates and passkey support, and raises the minimum Android and Apple platform versions. By Edin Kapić

It adds GraphQL subscription support, protocol-specific entrypoints, and an experimental defineNetwork API. Node.js interception now works at the TCP and TLS level.
